subtype: Feeling small at a friend's success [Receiver]
passage: Payal was stuck in a crawling auto in the rain, laptop bag soaked, a rejection email from that morning still open on her phone, when Vandana called. "Payal! I got it! Team lead!" Payal heard herself squeal, "Vandu, you deserve it!" And she meant it. She also felt something sharp and cold under her ribs. They had joined the company in the same month. After the call the auto still hadn't moved, and she let herself sit with it: I'm happy for her. I'm jealous. I'm scared I'm falling behind. All three. That evening she texted: "Honestly? I'm so proud of you, and also a bit jealous, because today was rough for me. But mostly proud. Dinner on me Saturday?" Vandana replied with a row of hearts and: "Thank you for telling me. Dinner on ME."

qa.q: What role did Vandana get?
qa.a: Team lead.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling after the call, stuck in the auto?
qa.a: Happy for Vandana, jealous, and scared of falling behind, all at once.

qa.q: Why did Payal's honest text leave room for real congratulation?
qa.a: By naming the jealousy and her rough day openly, she didn't have to fake anything, so "mostly proud" could be fully true.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt reading "also a bit jealous"?
qa.a: Vandana seems touched rather than hurt, thanking Payal for telling her and insisting on paying for dinner herself.

grounding: On a bad day, a young woman hears of her friend's promotion, feels happy and stung together, and admits both honestly.

subtype: Feeling small at a friend's success [Receiver]
passage: The terrace of Ira's building in Pune was strung with fairy lights, and everyone had phones out when Ira held up her hand and said, "We're engaged!" Aadhya screamed with the rest and hugged her hard. Then she went to refill the lemonade and stood by the water tank for a minute, breathing. Ira was her oldest friend. Ira was happy. And Aadhya felt, very suddenly, like the only one on the terrace still at the starting line. Later, when the others had left, Ira found her washing glasses. "You went quiet." Aadhya put down the glass. "I'm really happy for you. And a small, silly part of me feels left behind. I didn't want to hide it and be weird with you." Ira laughed and hugged her. "You're not behind. You're my maid of honour. Now dry these."

qa.q: Where was the engagement announced?
qa.a: On the terrace of Ira's building in Pune, under fairy lights.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya stand by the water tank for a minute?
qa.a: She needed to steady herself, suddenly feeling like the only one still at the starting line, even while happy for Ira.

qa.q: What did Aadhya choose to do when Ira said "You went quiet", and why did it help?
qa.a: She admitted both the happiness and the left-behind feeling, so she didn't have to act weird and the friendship stayed honest.

qa.q: How might Ira have felt hearing Aadhya's confession?
qa.a: Ira seems relieved and warm, laughing, hugging her, and reassuring her by naming her maid of honour.

grounding: A young woman is happy and stung at her best friend's engagement, and admitting both lets her celebrate genuinely.

passage:
"So? Say something!" Rajni was bouncing on the sofa. "Senior editor, Jas! Me!"
"That's huge. Congratulations," Jasleen said. The smile came out a bit stiff.
Rajni stopped bouncing. "You're doing the polite face."
"I'm not."
"You are. You did it when I got into college before you."
Jasleen let out a breath. "Okay. I'm really happy for you. And I'm also a bit stung. I applied for a senior role in March and didn't get it. That's not your fault."
"Oh, Jas." Rajni pulled her down onto the sofa. "Thank you for telling me instead of going weird for a month."
"I'd have gone weird for a month."
"I know. Now can I be excited?"
Jasleen grinned, properly this time. "Be excited. Senior editor! Where are we celebrating?"

qa.q: What role did Rajni get?
qa.a: Senior editor.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen's smile come out a bit stiff?
qa.a: She was happy but stung, because she had applied for a senior role in March and didn't get it.

qa.q: What choice turned the conversation around?
qa.a: Jasleen admitted both feelings instead of keeping the polite face, and saying it wasn't Rajni's fault let them celebrate honestly.

qa.q: How does Rajni seem to feel about Jasleen's honesty?
qa.a: Rajni seems grateful, preferring to hear it straight rather than have Jasleen go weird for a month.

grounding: A young woman feels both glad and stung at a close friend's promotion, and saying so openly frees her to celebrate properly.

subtype: Feeling small at a friend's success [Receiver]
passage: I'm Anand. Last spring Nilesh and I were both line cooks at the same restaurant, two years in, same burn marks on our wrists. Then the owner made Nilesh sous chef. He pulled me into the cold room to tell me first, eyes shining. I hugged him and meant it. Then I went home and scrubbed an already clean pan for twenty minutes. For a week I was too cheerful, all "Yes, Chef!" jokes, and Nilesh kept giving me odd looks. Finally, over staff dinner, I said it. "I'm really happy for you. And it stings a bit, because I wanted it too. Both are true." Nilesh put down his fork. "Thank God. I thought you were angry with me." We both laughed. Then I said congratulations again, properly this time, and it came out lighter.

qa.q: What job did the owner give Nilesh?
qa.a: Sous chef.

qa.q: What does scrubbing an already clean pan for twenty minutes suggest about Anand's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Anand was stung and restless underneath the real happiness, with nowhere to put the mixed feelings yet.

qa.q: What choice at staff dinner changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: Anand admitted being happy and stung at once instead of over-cheering, which cleared the air so the second congratulations could be genuine.

qa.q: How had the week of "Yes, Chef!" jokes looked to Nilesh?
qa.a: Nilesh sensed something was off and feared Anand was angry, so the honest admission came as a relief 😅

grounding: A young adult whose close friend is promoted feels happy and stung together, and admitting both honestly makes real congratulation possible.

subtype: Feeling small at a friend's success [Receiver]
passage:
Coach's note, city athletics club, Saturday.
The selection list arrived this morning: Uma is in the state relay squad. Dolma is not. They have trained side by side for three years. Dolma hugged Uma first, loudly and fast, then went off to run extra laps nobody had set. I let her run. Afterwards she sat on the bench, untying and retying one shoe. I asked how she was. She said, "I'm so happy for her. I'm also jealous, and I hate that." I told her both can sit together, and saying it is better than hiding it. At the end of practice she went over to Uma again, slower this time, and said something I couldn't hear. Uma laughed and cried a little. I have booked a session with Dolma on Tuesday to plan next season.

qa.q: How long have Dolma and Uma trained side by side?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: What does Dolma untying and retying one shoe suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was unsettled, caught between feelings she hadn't sorted out yet: happy for Uma and stung at the same time.

qa.q: What helped Dolma move from a fast hug to a real congratulation?
qa.a: Saying the jealousy out loud and hearing that both feelings can sit together let her return to Uma calmly and congratulate her properly.

qa.q: How might Uma have experienced the two hugs?
qa.a: The first, quick hug may have felt a little hollow; the slower second talk likely felt real, which is why Uma laughed and cried 🤍

grounding: A coach sees an athlete feel both glad and jealous when her training partner is selected, admit it honestly, and then offer a genuine congratulation.
